name: Omar Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of four men on the home farm at the Ashcombe Estate, an old family estate that owns most of the land round our village. We've got four hundred hectares of wheat and oilseed, six hundred ewes and some beef cattle. I've been there sixteen years, so I'm the one who sets the young lads off in the morning, then I'm usually on the sprayer or the drill myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy drilling in autumn when the ground's right and the lines come out straight, there's a pride in that. The hard part is the wage, which is fair for farming but farming doesn't pay. Claire works in the school kitchen and between us we cover the mortgage on our house on Church Street and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about right. It's a useful tool, the estate office uses it for the paperwork and I use it now and then to write up the spray records, but it was never going to farm the land. Good honest work still needs a man on the tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief. I've got sixteen years in, I know the estate, and I'm not keen on starting over at forty-three. Nothing changing suits me, though I'd still like a better wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as normal. I'd keep using the AI for the records, it saves me an evening a month. And I'd keep pushing the estate manager to take on an apprentice, because the lads we get now don't stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you want an apprentice so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because nobody taught the last two lads properly and they left within a year. I was taught by old Jim, who'd been on the estate forty years. You learn the land from someone, not from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still like a better wage. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay something off the mortgage and get Noah a decent bike for his paper round. And maybe take Claire away for a weekend, which we haven't done since Sophie was born.

S0.say: AI is a useful tool for paperwork and spray records, but it was never going to farm the land. Good honest work still needs someone on the tractor.
S0.think: It's a relief, because after sixteen years on the estate he isn't keen on starting over at 43. He'd still like a better wage.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and uses AI for spray records, saving an evening a month. Keeps pushing the estate manager to take on a proper apprentice.
S0.quote: You learn the land from someone, not from a screen.
S0.fieldNote: He uses AI casually for paperwork and sees no conflict with his traditional views. His real passion is passing on skills through apprenticeships, rooted in his own training. He mentions small, specific things he'd do with more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of farming and we'll adapt like our fathers did. But I'd also say young people need proper apprenticeships, not just online courses. I'd say it after church and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the estate would cut from four men to two within a few years. They'd keep the ones who can run the new machines. I'd want to make sure I'm one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till the estate brings in the first self-driving tractor, then ask to be the one trained on it. I'd watch how other estates do it first, there's one over the hill that's always first. And I'd put a bit aside each month, even fifty, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the back of my mind when I see the estate manager walking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be the two to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably young Ben, who's only been there eighteen months, and Pete, who's sixty and might take early retirement. That's how they'd do it, the soft way. I'd feel bad for Ben.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to the estate about Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep him and train him, he's got good hands. But it's their land and their money. I'd say it once and leave it.

S1.say: Change is part of farming, and people will adapt as their fathers did. Young people need proper apprenticeships, not just online courses.
S1.think: He expects the estate to cut from four workers to two within a few years, keeping those who can run the new machines. He intends to be one of them.
S1.do: Waits until the estate brings in its first self-driving tractor, then asks to be trained on it. Watches how a neighbouring estate does it first and saves fifty a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, especially when he sees the estate manager walking over.
S1.quote: It's in the back of my mind when I see the estate manager walking over.
S1.fieldNote: He accepts the estate's right to decide as owners, which fits his free-market views. He'd speak up for a younger colleague once and then let it go. His plan is to wait until change is proven and then step forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has been forced on people by big tech companies and the government let it happen. Families and churches will have to look after each other. I'd say people need work, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is no time. If robots can do all four jobs on the estate, the family will do the sums like any business and we're gone. I don't blame them, but I'd have nowhere to go, there's no other farm work round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut straight away: the satellite TV, the takeaway, Noah's new bike. I'd ask the estate for a reference and any work they had, hedging or fencing or keeping the gardens. And I'd ask at church whether anyone knew of work, because that's how jobs have always been found round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd failed Claire and the kids, even though it's not my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you feel like you'd failed, if it's not your fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a man provides for his family, that's how I was raised. It doesn't matter whose fault it is when the mortgage letter comes. I know that's old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noah about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to find something with his hands that a robot can't do, but in this picture I don't know what that is. So I'd tell him to work hard and keep his faith. That's all I'd have.

S2.say: This has been forced on people by big tech companies with the government letting it happen. Families and churches will need to look after each other, and people need work, not handouts.
S2.think: Two years is no time, and the estate would do the sums like any business and let the workers go. He wouldn't blame them but would have nowhere to go locally.
S2.do: Cuts the television subscription, the takeaway and his son's new bike immediately. Asks the estate for a reference and any odd work, and asks at church about jobs.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and feeling he'd failed his family even though it wouldn't be his fault.
S2.quote: It doesn't matter whose fault it is when the mortgage letter comes.
S2.fieldNote: His sense of being the provider makes the fast scenario feel like personal failure. He blames tech companies and government, not the estate, which he treats as a business with the right to cut. His advice to his son runs out because he can't see what work would remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to get ready, but they'll need proper training schemes, run by employers, not just government courses. I'd say the estates should take responsibility for their own people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to get qualified on the machines and maybe a second trade. I'd be forty-eight, still working, still with a mortgage. I'd rather be ready than hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do the self-driving machinery course at the agricultural college the estate's used before. I'd look at a part-time course in hedge-laying and dry-stone walling, because the estates always need that and robots are clumsy at it. And I'd save harder, a hundred a month if we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with it, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hedge-laying and walling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's slow, skilled and no two are the same. Old Jim taught me a bit, I'd like to learn it properly. I could see myself doing it until I'm seventy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to help with the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if the college used it. I use it for the spray records already, so I'm not against it. I'd just want a real person checking my work at the end.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to get ready, but people need proper employer-run training schemes rather than government courses. Estates should take responsibility for their own workers.
S3.think: Five years gives him time to qualify on the new machines and maybe learn a second trade. He'd rather be ready than hope.
S3.do: Takes a self-driving machinery course at the agricultural college in the first year and a part-time hedge-laying and dry-stone walling course. Saves a hundred a month if the household can manage it.
S3.feel: Anxious, but having something to do helps.
S3.quote: I could see myself doing it until I'm seventy.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he sees a path through traditional skilled crafts that machines struggle with. He's comfortable using AI in training but wants a person to check his work. He places responsibility on employers rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time that nobody has an excuse. Apprenticeships, family businesses, people helping each other. That's how communities got through the last big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and I'd have the walling and hedging to fall back on. It's Noah and Sophie I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the machinery course early, then the walling course. I'd talk to the estate about an apprenticeship scheme, with me teaching the young ones while I still can. And I'd sit down with Noah about what he wants to do, because he'd be choosing right as it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's far enough off to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want Noah to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's good with engines, so maybe a mechanic or an electrician apprenticeship. Something he learns from someone. I'd rather he had a trade than a degree that doesn't lead anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'while I still can' about teaching. Do you think that job goes too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the robots can do it all, what's there to teach? But people will still want to learn how things are done properly, like they still learn to ride horses.

S4.say: Ten years leaves nobody an excuse, and communities should rely on apprenticeships, family businesses and helping each other, as they did through earlier changes.
S4.think: He expects to be all right at 53 with the children grown and hedging and walling skills to fall back on. His real concern is his children's futures.
S4.do: Takes the machinery course early and then the walling course, and proposes an estate apprenticeship scheme with himself teaching. Talks with his son about trade apprenticeships.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, since it's far enough off to plan.
S4.quote: But people will still want to learn how things are done properly, like they still learn to ride horses.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his focus moves to teaching and his children's trades. He sees traditional crafts surviving the way horse riding has. He admits even teaching might go, and answers with a belief in tradition rather than certainty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there'd be no time to learn anything new before the estate had to cut. What would help is the estates and the employers paying for training while we still have jobs, and apprenticeships for the young ones, so it's not all on the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Hedges, walls, ditches, the old ways of looking after the land. If the robots just farm it for money, somebody still needs to care for it like it's going to be here in a hundred years.

headlineQuote: Somebody still needs to care for it like it's going to be here in a hundred years.
portrait: Omar Dubois is 43 and has worked sixteen years as the senior hand on the Ashcombe Estate home farm, with crops, sheep and beef cattle, while his wife Claire works in a school kitchen. He is traditional, churchgoing and believes in apprenticeships and work over handouts, and he uses AI now and then for spray records. He is calm when AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, planning to be trained on the first self-driving tractor. AGI in two years leaves him alarmed and feeling he'd failed as a provider. With five or ten years he retrains in machinery and in hedge-laying and walling, and hopes to teach the next generation.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be no time to learn anything new before the estate had to cut workers.
whatWouldHelp: Employers paying for training while people still have jobs, and apprenticeships for young people, so it isn't all left to the government.
